questions.question: For a queueing system with $L(t)$ jobs present at time $t$ and job $k$ arriving at time $A_k$, what does the arrival-average state probability $\pi(n)$ measure?
options: The long-run fraction of time during which exactly $n$ jobs are present in the system.
The probability that the system holds exactly $n$ jobs at one fixed, very large time $t$.
The long-run fraction of arriving jobs that find exactly $n$ jobs already in the system.
The long-run fraction of arriving jobs that bring the number in the system up to $n$.

questions.question: The arrival-average state probability $\pi(n)$ records job $k$, arriving at time $A_k$, through the left limit $L(A_k-)$ rather than the value $L(A_k)$. Why is the left limit used?
options: Because $L$ jumps up at $A_k$, so $L(A_k)$ already counts the arriving job itself.
Because $L$ is undefined at the arrival epoch $A_k$, so only a limit can be taken there.
Because $L(A_k-)$ also includes the jobs that are departing at that same instant.
Because the left limit averages the values of $L$ just before and just after $A_k$.

questions.question: Let $A(t)$ be the number of arrivals in $[0,t]$ and $A(n,t)$ the number of those arrivals that find $n$ jobs present. Why does $\sum_{n\ge0}A(n,t)=A(t)$ hold for every $t$?
options: Because the fractions $A(n,t)/A(t)$ converge as $t\to\infty$ and their limits sum to one.
Because the system spends all of the time in $[0,t]$ in some state, so the times add up to $t$.
Because each arriving job is counted once for every state that it passes through while queueing.
Because each arrival finds the system in exactly one state, so it is counted in exactly one $A(n,t)$.

questions.question: For a queue with arrival times $A_k$, the quantity $A(n,t)=\sum_{k=1}^{A(t)}\mathbf{1}\{L(A_k-)=n\}$ is defined, where $A(t)$ is the number of arrivals in $[0,t]$. What does $A(n,t)$ count?
options: The total time in $[0,t]$ during which exactly $n$ jobs are present in the system.
The number of arrivals in $[0,t]$ that find exactly $n$ jobs present when they arrive.
The fraction of arrivals in $[0,t]$ that find exactly $n$ jobs present when they arrive.
The number of arrivals in $[0,t]$ after which exactly $n$ jobs are present in the system.

questions.question: An analyst wants an empirical estimate of $\pi(0)$, the long-run fraction of arriving jobs that find a single-server system empty, from one long sample path. Which procedure gives it?
options: Inspect the system at the fixed times $1,2,3,\ldots$ and record how often it is empty.
Record the fraction of the observation period during which no job is present.
Ask every arriving job whether it found the system empty, and record the fraction of yes.
Count the arrivals that find the system empty and divide by the length of the period.

questions.question: Ten arriving jobs record the numbers of jobs they find just before entering: $0,2,1,1,0,3,1,0,0,2$. What is the empirical arrival-average fraction for state $1$, that is $A(1,t)/A(t)$?

At a single first-come-first-served server, jobs arrive at times $1,3,4,7$ and leave at times $2,5,6.5,8$ in the same order. How many jobs does job $3$, arriving at time $4$, find in the system, that is $L(4-)$?

Jobs arrive one at a time and no departure occurs at an arrival epoch. Just after the five arrivals, the right-continuous values are $L(A_k)=1,2,1,1,3$. What is the average number of jobs these arrivals found?

At a single server, jobs arrive at times $6,12,18,\ldots$ and every job needs exactly $4$ time units of service. What is the arrival-average probability $\pi(0)$ that an arriving job finds the system empty?
Jobs arrive at times $1,2,4,6$ and find $0,1,1,0$ jobs present, respectively. Using only arrivals in $[0,5]$, what is the empirical fraction $A(1,5)/A(5)$ of arrivals that find exactly one job?

Two sample paths of a queue have the same arrival times and the same values $L(A_k-)$ at every arrival, but between arrivals the paths spend different amounts of time in each state. What follows for $\pi(n)$ and $p(n)$?
options: Both $\pi(n)$ and $p(n)$ agree on the two paths, as they describe the same jobs.
Both may differ, because $\pi(n)$ is built from $p(n)$ by weighting time intervals.
$p(n)$ is the same on both paths, while the arrival averages can change.
$\pi(n)$ agrees on the two paths, whereas $p(n)$ may differ between them.

questions.question: A system spends a positive long-run fraction of time with exactly $2$ jobs present, but no job ever arrives while $2$ jobs are present. What is the arrival-average probability $\pi(2)$, assuming the limits exist?
options: $\pi(2)=0$, even though $p(2)>0$, since no arrival finds two jobs present.
$\pi(2)=p(2)$, since every state that is visited is seen by some arrival.
$\pi(2)>0$, since the arrivals that raise the level to $2$ are counted for state $2$.
$\pi(2)$ is undefined, since $A(2,t)=0$ for every $t$ and it cannot be divided.

questions.question: The arrival average $\pi(n)$ can be written as $\lim_{t\to\infty}A(n,t)/A(t)$ or as $\lim_{N\to\infty}N^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}\{L(A_k-)=n\}$. Under which condition on the arrival count $A(t)$ do the two forms agree?
options: When $A(t)/t$ tends to zero, so that arrivals become rare over time.
When $A(t)$ is bounded, so that only finitely many arrivals have to be counted.
When $A(t)\to\infty$, so that letting $t$ grow also lets the number of jobs grow.
When $A(t)\le t$ for every $t$, so that there is at most one arrival per time unit.

questions.question: At a single server observed over a long period, $A(t)=200$ arrivals are recorded and $A(0,t)=150$ of them find the system empty; the server log shows that the system was empty during $40\%$ of the period. Which reading of these data is correct?
options: $p(0)\approx0.75$ and $\pi(0)\approx0.4$, since the arrival data describe how often the server is idle.
$\pi(0)\approx0.75$ and $p(0)\approx0.4$; the arrivals tend to come at moments when the system is empty.
$p(0)\approx0.4$ and $\pi(0)\approx0.75\cdot0.4=0.3$, since an arrival finds the system empty only during idle time.
$\pi(0)\approx0.75$, so $p(0)$ must also be about $0.75$ and the $40\%$ in the server log must be an error.

questions.question: Jobs arrive at a single server: the first at time $A_1=1$, and then $A_k=A_{k-1}+X_k$ with inter-arrival times $X_2,X_3,X_4,X_5=1,1,3,1$. The five jobs leave at times $3.5,4.5,5.5,6.5,8$. What fraction of the five arrivals find the system empty?
Out of $40$ arrivals, $12$ find $0$ jobs present, $18$ find $1$, $6$ find $2$ and $4$ find $3$. What is the average number of jobs found by an arrival, $N^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{N}L(A_k-)$ with $N=40$?
Jobs arrive faster than a single server can serve them, so $L(t)\to\infty$ and, for each fixed $n$, only finitely many arrivals find exactly $n$ jobs. What follows for the arrival averages $\pi(n)$?
options: Every $\pi(n)$ is positive, because each state $n$ is found by at least one arrival.
The limits fail to exist, because $A(n,t)$ stops growing while $A(t)$ keeps growing.
Every $\pi(n)=0$, so $\sum_n\pi(n)=0$ although $\sum_n A(n,t)/A(t)=1$ for every $t$.
The $\pi(n)$ still sum to one, because the fractions sum to one at every finite time $t$.

questions.question: For a single-server queue, it is known only that $\pi(0)=1$: in the long run every arriving job finds the system empty. What can be concluded about the time-average idle fraction $p(0)$?
options: $p(0)=1$, because a server that is never found busy must be idle all the time.
Nothing beyond $0\le p(0)\le1$; $p(0)$ can be arbitrarily close to $0$.
$p(0)\ge1/2$, because jobs never wait and so the server is idle at least half the time.
$p(0)$ must equal the fraction of arrivals that find exactly one job present.

questions.question: A sample path on $[0,10]$ has $L(t)=0,1,2,1,2,3,2,1,0$ on the intervals $[0,1),[1,2),[2,3),[3,5),[5,6),[6,7),[7,8),[8,9),[9,10]$; jumps are single arrivals or departures. What is the average number of jobs found by the arrivals?
Jobs arrive at times $0,1,2,\ldots$ at a single first-come-first-served server; their service times repeat the cycle $1.5,0.2,0.2$, so the mean service time is below the gap of $1$. What is $\pi(0)$?
